cards.title: Near-optimal explicit binary linear codes for erasure list decoding
cards.formal: Construct explicit binary linear codes with near-optimal rate and list size for adversarial erasure list decoding. Concretely, for a surviving fraction 0<τ≤1 and block length N, a code C≤F₂^N of dimension K should have at most L codewords consistent with every assignment of binary values to any set of at least ⌈τN⌉ coordinates; its rate is R=K/N. The source asks for near-optimal linear codes after constructing nonlinear ones, but does not specify the required functions R(τ), L(τ), or the regime relating τ and N. It therefore does not yet state one quantitative construction theorem.
cards.why: Explicit binary linear codes with sharp erasure tradeoffs would combine simple algebraic encoding with strong guarantees against adversarial information loss. The question also tests the cost of linearity relative to the source’s nonlinear constructions.
cards.status_note: Read the 2020 model, rank criterion, theorem and exact question; checked the November 2025 local-property revision and the erasure-ensemble theorem. Searches through 12 September 2026 found related list-recovery and larger-alphabet work but no source-specified numerical target that can be certified as solved or still open here.

progress.text: The nonlinear construction achieves the stated near-linear rate exponent and polylogarithmic lists, and explicitly leaves the linear-code question open.

New explicit constructions address local code properties over enlarged alphabets, while a separate result obtains strong per-pattern guarantees from ensembles. Their models differ from this binary single-code target.

sentences: The target is a single explicit binary linear code that keeps only a small list of possible messages after adversarial erasures.
Its parameters are the surviving coordinate fraction, encoding rate and maximum list size.
The source’s nonlinear construction achieves a list-size advantage that cannot simply be required of linear codes.
It does not specify the desired linear rate/list tradeoff or the full parameter and construction regime.
Later larger-alphabet and code-ensemble results are recorded with their different guarantees, while the missing benchmark choices remain explicit.

cards.definitions: F₂={0,1} with arithmetic modulo 2. A binary linear [N,K] code is the image of an injective linear encoding m↦mG, where m∈F₂^K and the K×N generator matrix G has rank K. Its block length is N and rate is K/N. For T⊆[N] and z∈F₂^T, let C(T,z)={c∈C: c|_T=z}. Erasure list decoding with surviving fraction τ and maximum list size L means |C(T,z)|≤L for every T with |T|≥⌈τN⌉ and every z. The erased coordinates are known to the decoder; surviving values must match exactly. The guarantee is worst-case over coordinate sets and values, not a probability over random erasures. If G_T is the submatrix of columns indexed by T, then every nonempty C(T,z) has exactly 2^{K−rank(G_T)} elements, so the property is equivalent to 2^{K−rank(G_T)}≤L for all such T. It is enough to check |T|=⌈τN⌉ because revealing more coordinates cannot increase the list. L is a positive integer. The source’s explicitness concerns encoding, whereas a separate concluding question concerns efficient decoding of its nonlinear construction. For a linear code, a displayed generator matrix permits encoding by binary matrix multiplication; an explicit family still needs a uniform algorithm to produce or access its generators with a stated resource bound. No such near-optimal family specification is fixed by the extracted sentence.
cards.answer_criterion: After fixing admissible N,τ and the required rate, list bound and construction time, provide one uniform binary-linear code construction meeting those guarantees for every admissible parameter choice, with proofs; or prove that the specified conjunction is impossible. The source passage currently leaves those quantitative choices unresolved. A larger-alphabet code, a nonlinear code, or an ensemble whose successful member depends on the erasure pattern does not meet the same single-code binary-linear requirement.

context_blocks.title: What the 2020 nonlinear result achieves
context_blocks.text: For every fixed 0<γ<1 and an inverse-polynomial surviving fraction in its message-length regime, the source constructs an explicitly encodable binary code of rate τ^{1+γ} and list size log^{O_γ(1)}(1/τ). This is an erasure result, not the corresponding adversarial bit-error problem.

context_blocks.title: Linearity changes the attainable list size
context_blocks.text: The paper records Guruswami’s Ω(1/τ) list-size obstruction for the linear-code regime under discussion and stresses that its much smaller lists use nonlinearity. Its request for near-optimal linear codes must therefore be judged against linear-code tradeoffs, not by copying the nonlinear parameter pair.

context_blocks.title: Explicit construction does not automatically preserve a binary alphabet
context_blocks.text: A November 2025 preprint gives explicit erasure-list-recovery constructions with rate and list parameters comparable to random linear codes, but enlarges the alphabet by a parameter-dependent amount. The alphabet remains constant with block length; that does not make it binary. Corollary 6.13 in the checked revision is the relevant erasure result.

context_blocks.title: Ensembles have a different quantifier order
context_blocks.text: Another 2025 preprint constructs constant-size ensembles over any fixed alphabet near the Singleton rate. For each erasure pattern, most codes in the ensemble correct it. This does not assert that one member corrects every pattern, or give the requested small-list property for a single binary code.

cards.context:
For every fixed 0<γ<1 and an inverse-polynomial surviving fraction in its message-length regime, the source constructs an explicitly encodable binary code of rate τ^{1+γ} and list size log^{O_γ(1)}(1/τ). This is an erasure result, not the corresponding adversarial bit-error problem.

The paper records Guruswami’s Ω(1/τ) list-size obstruction for the linear-code regime under discussion and stresses that its much smaller lists use nonlinearity. Its request for near-optimal linear codes must therefore be judged against linear-code tradeoffs, not by copying the nonlinear parameter pair.

A November 2025 preprint gives explicit erasure-list-recovery constructions with rate and list parameters comparable to random linear codes, but enlarges the alphabet by a parameter-dependent amount. The alphabet remains constant with block length; that does not make it binary. Corollary 6.13 in the checked revision is the relevant erasure result.

Another 2025 preprint constructs constant-size ensembles over any fixed alphabet near the Singleton rate. For each erasure pattern, most codes in the ensemble correct it. This does not assert that one member corrects every pattern, or give the requested small-list property for a single binary code.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
